analysis.one_liner: Cuts off federal payments to individuals and corporations once their income tops $120,000, to shrink the deficit.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: one senator sponsored it, no one else joined, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the federal government from making any payment that pushed an individual's income above $120,000 a year, a corporation's taxable income above $120,000, or a tax-exempt organization's total receipts above $620,000. In plain terms, it would have ended federal checks to wealthy retirees, farm subsidies and contract payments to large companies, and most federal grants to large nonprofits. Its stated purpose was to close the budget deficit on the backs of the best-off recipients rather than program cuts across the board.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers generally, through a smaller deficit, and lower-income recipients of federal programs who would have been spared from sharing in cuts, since payments to people under the income limits would have been untouched.

how_it_helps.text: Bars any federal payment that would lift an individual's adjusted gross income above $120,000 per year ($60,000 for a married person filing separately), including payments to a spouse or dependents counted as one unit [S3].

Bars federal payments to any company or other private entity once its taxable income exceeds $120,000, and caps payments to tax-exempt organizations and foreign-taxed persons at $120,000 or gross receipts of $620,000 [S3].
The stated aim is deficit reduction by eliminating mandatory payments to wealthy individuals and large corporations rather than cutting benefits for everyone [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy individuals who receive federal payments (for example, high-income Social Security recipients or farm payment recipients), large corporations receiving federal money, and large tax-exempt institutions such as hospitals, universities, and charities with receipts over $620,000.

drawbacks.text: The cap on tax-exempt organizations is blunt: a nonprofit hospital, university, or research institution whose gross receipts exceed $620,000 would be cut off from federal payments entirely, which could end Medicare reimbursements to large nonprofit hospitals and federal research grants to universities [S3].

Because the bill caps any payment to any private entity with taxable income over $120,000, it would sweep in payments far beyond classic subsidies to the wealthy, potentially interrupting government payments to mid-sized businesses in the middle of a contract year [S3].

A good-faith objection: means-testing payments at $120,000 raises relatively little money compared with the deficit, and a flat cutoff can create sharp cliffs in which a recipient loses an entire payment rather than a proportional share.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — stop sending federal checks to people and companies who do not need them — is popular and straightforward, and it protects ordinary recipients entirely. But the bill was drafted so broadly that it would have cut off federal money to large hospitals, universities, and charities, not just to genuinely wealthy individuals and corporate subsidy programs, and it appears to have been a statement bill rather than a workable drafting exercise.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in early October 1992, read twice, sent to the Governmental Affairs Committee, and nothing further happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Hank Brown of Colorado introduced the bill on October 5, 1992, seven weeks before the end of the 102nd Congress [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Governmental Affairs, where it stayed [S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill received no committee action, no floor vote, and no House companion action [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy individuals, large corporations, and big tax-exempt institutions continue receiving federal payments that the bill would have ended. Deficit reduction through cutting payments to the best-off recipients did not happen; the committee that never acted on the bill faced no political cost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-income recipients and large federal contractors

for.name: Sen. Hank Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to committee; no senator joined him as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never had a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican introduced the bill with zero cosponsors of either party, so the record shows no party bloc ever lined up for or against it.

industries.industry: Large corporations receiving federal payments (defense contractors, agribusiness, subsidy recipients)
industries.note: The bill would cut off federal payments to any company once its taxable income passed $120,000, ending subsidies and contract payments to profitable firms. Their interest in keeping those payments runs against taxpayers who would otherwise bear the deficit.

Organizations with gross receipts over $620,000 would lose federal payments, including things like Medicare reimbursements and research grants, while still delivering public services. Many do serve the public directly, so the cut falls on institutions as well as the people who use them.

Anyone whose income would exceed $120,000 with a federal payment would become ineligible, ending benefits like high-income Social Security checks. Losing a check is a cost to them, but the bill's whole premise is that these payments are unnecessary.
